A report can be a written or spoken description of a situation or event, giving people the information they need.
A written report includes different elements.

1. A title page which includes a title, the author's name and the date it was written.
  2. A summary which includes a short overview on what the report is about.
  3. An introduction.
  4. A body which includes subtitles that provide information about the different sections in the body.
  5. A conclusion which wraps up what you talked about in your report.

Title: The Changing Face of Inuit Identity in the 21st Century
Author: Richard Rice
Date: August 21st 2016
Summary: Balancing Inuit culture and identity within modern day influences can be challenging.
Introduction: This report looks at how some aspects of Inuit culture have remained the same, while others have changed quite drastically with the times.
Subtitles within the Body: Music, Education, Art, Language
Conclusion:  This experience has changed all my perception of Inuit life.
Go online and find information about a culture that is trying to blend their culture with 21st century expectations.
Imagine you visit their community and write a 150-200 word report on their culture and experience in modern society.
Write about unusual or unique event in the Present Perfect tense. Include words like until, now, and yet.
Read your report to a partner.
I find information about a different culture online.
I write a report about the experiences of a different culture.
I write about unusual or unique events.

Writing a Report about Unusual Events
You use the Present Perfect tense when you want to write about unusual events.

You use the Present Perfect tense in a variety of ways:

  1. To talk about actions that recently started and may have finished recently or may be continuing. It is normally clear from the context. You use words like just, only just and recently in these constructions.
    For example:
    Recently, I have traveled to Nunavut after being hounded by a journalist on why I hadn't been to this part of Canada yet. I have only just arrived and I have realized that while some aspects of Inuit culture have remained the same, others have changed quite drastically with the times.

1. To talk or ask about experience or your opinion based on experience. You use the word ever in questions. You also use the word yet in negatives and in questions.
    For example:
    Do you think things will ever be the same?
    Have you been to Nunavut yet?
    I haven't yet seen that part of Canada.
Up to now, the older community members have been a source of wisdom and learning.
Recently, I have traveled to Nunavut after being hounded by a journalist on why I hadn't been to this part of Canada yet.
You have seen so many changes yet you have shown so much inner strength.
I haven't noticed a change until now.
I have only just arrived and I have realized that while some aspects of Inuit culture have remained the same, others have changed quite drastically with the times.

images.text: Recently, I have traveled to Nunavut after being hounded by a journalist on why I hadn't been to this part of Canada yet. I imagined that my one-week stay would involve sleeping in an igloo, traveling around on a dogsled, and hunting for seal. By spending some time with these people, I changed all my previous perceptions of Inuit life. I have only just arrived and I have realized that while some aspects of Inuit culture have remained the same, others have changed quite drastically with the times.

The Inuit today generally live in modern homes, watch TV, listen to popular music, and use the Internet. Motorized sleds called skidoos have replaced dogsleds. Whereas in the past the Inuit spent most of their time working to survive, there is a 60% unemployment rate amongst the Inuit today. Recently, this has been a source of considerable stress, and has represented one of the biggest problems in Inuit society.

After eating a delicious dinner of game bird with the Eejeesiak family, I talked about the changes in the community and in Inuit culture. Before leaving I asked, “Do you think things will ever be the same?” She explained to me that, “one of the most upsetting changes has been the relationship between young and old people. Up to now, the older community members have been a source of wisdom and learning. Recently, the young people  have been  too influenced by cultures outside the Inuit communities ... which obviously changes the society as a whole.” I then asked, “You have seen so many changes, yet you have so much inner strength."  She answered that it was their love and respect for the family and for others in the community that allows them to endure. “Things may have changed,” she explained. “But by working together to maintain our core values, respect for each other and for the land, we will always remain.”
